ROOT CAUSE DETERMINATION\\n\\nThe synthetic evidence points to a dependency saturation event as the primary cause of the queue incident. The causal chain is visible in the timeline: the system was stable at 09:00 with a queue depth of 120 and 8 workers (E01). By 09:10, queue depth had exploded to 1,850 while the worker count was unchanged at 8 (E02), and median latency rose roughly eightfold from 1.8s to 14.2s by 09:12 (E03). Critically, at 09:15 outbound dependency B began returning HTTP 429 (rate limit) responses for 31% of requests (E05). At 09:26, disabling retries against dependency B caused queue depth to drop 38% in six minutes (E08), and at 09:35 raising dependency B's rate limits drove 429s below 1%, after which queue depth returned below 150 within eleven minutes (E09). This before/after intervention pattern — the problem clears when the dependency constraint is removed — is the strongest causal signature in the evidence and establishes dependency B's rate limiting as the primary cause, with retry amplification as the chief amplifier.\\n\\nIt is worth noting the sequencing: queue depth rose (E02, 09:10) and latency rose (E03, 09:12) before 429s were logged at 09:15 (E05). The most consistent interpretation is that 429 responses, retries, and elevated per-task latency began earlier than the explicit 09:15 observation, which likely marks the point at which the 31% failure share was first measured and recorded rather than the exact onset. Alternatively, latency degradation may have started milliseconds before the rate limiter tripped, as B's upstream components (connection pools, GC pauses) degraded under rising load. This ambiguity does not change the causal verdict: the only interventions that recovered the system both targeted dependency B (E08, E09).\\n\\n2. PRIMARY CAUSE VS. AMPLIFIERS\\n\\nPrimary cause: dependency B rate limiting (HTTP 429 at 31% of requests, E05), remedied directly by raising B's limits (E09).\\n\\nAmplifiers:\\n(a) Retry policy. A 420% increase in retry volume (E06) with exponential backoff capped at three retries multiplied effective demand on B. Retries against a rate-limited dependency are anti-amplifying: they consume quota that would otherwise serve fresh work, deepening the 429 share. Disabling retries alone recovered 38% of queue depth (E08), proving retries were a major amplifier, though not the primary cause.\\n(b) Latency feedback loop. 14.2s median latency (E03) slowed per-task completion, holding tasks in worker slots longer, which raised effective queue depth independently of arrival rate.\\n\\n3. WHY ADDING WORKERS FAILED\\n\\nAt 09:20, doubling workers from 8 to 16 reduced queue depth only 6% in ten minutes (E07). This is expected and diagnostic. The bottleneck was not local concurrency: CPU was 43%, memory 51%, disk 22% (E04) — the hosts were far from saturation. Adding workers increased the number of tasks concurrently blocked on dependency B and its rate limiter. B's 429s are a fixed-capacity resource; more workers simply created more contention against the same quota and, via retries, more 429s. The 6% improvement likely came from a marginal overlap gain and reduced latency-induced serialization, but the dependency ceiling dominated. E07 plus E04 together rule out resource exhaustion and local worker starvation as the bottleneck.\\n\\n4. RETRY POLICY ASSESSMENT\\n\\nExponential backoff with a maximum of three retries is a reasonable default for transient errors, but it is misapplied here. HTTP 429 responses frequently carry a Retry-After header; honoring it, or at minimum applying a client-side token-bucket budget per dependency, is required. Three retries at 31% failure rates and 420% retry volume growth (E06) produced a retry storm that prolonged the incident. Recommended policy: (i) treat 429 as non-retryable by the general retry path — instead shed, defer, or route to a dedicated rate-limited queue; (ii) honor Retry-After strictly; (iii) apply per-dependency concurrency limits and circuit breaking so retries auto-suspend when 429 share exceeds a threshold; (iv) add jitter to prevent retry synchronization.\\n\\n5. ALTERNATIVE HYPOTHESES AND WHY THEY ARE LESS SUPPORTED\\n\\nHypothesis A (preferred): dependency B rate limiting with retry amplification. Directly supported by E05, E08, E09.\\nHypothesis B: local resource exhaustion or worker starvation. Rejected because CPU/memory/disk were well below saturation (E04) and doubling workers barely helped (E07). If workers were starved for CPU, the added workers should have scaled throughput; they did not.\\nHypothesis C: an upstream arrival-rate surge (traffic spike) drove the queue. Possible in principle — queue depth rose before 429s were logged (E02 vs E05) — but E10 confirms no deploy, schema, restart, route, or credential change in the window, and the recovery evidence ties outcomes to B's capacity, not to arrival rate: depth fell when retries were disabled (E08) and when B's limits were raised (E09), with no observed change in ingress. A pure traffic surge would not have responded so decisively to B-side fixes. A modest surge may have triggered B's limiter, but B's quota is still the proximate cause.\\nHypothesis D: network fault to B. E10 excludes route changes, and the symptom is specifically 429 (an application-level rate-limit signal), not timeouts or connection errors; a network fault would not clear by raising rate limits (E09).\\n\\n6. UNCERTAINTIES\\n\\nThe evidence lacks arrival-rate metrics, dependency B's quota configuration and 429 onset timestamp, per-task retry distributions, and Retry-After header handling. The 09:15 timestamp likely reflects first measurement of the 31% share rather than true onset. Recovery metrics lack arrival-rate context, so demand-versus-capacity decomposition at 09:35 is approximate.\\n\\n7. STAGED REMEDIATION PLAN\\n\\nStage 1 (immediate, 0-24h): disable or heavily curtail retries on 429 for dependency B (validated by E08); add alerting on 429 share and retry amplification ratio; confirm runbooks route on-call to check dependency health before scaling workers.\\nStage 2 (short-term, 1-2 weeks): implement per-dependency rate limiting, token-bucket budgeting, and circuit breakers; honor Retry-After; coordinate with dependency B's owners on quota headroom and burst policy (E09 shows quota headroom is the decisive lever).\\nStage 3 (medium-term, 2-6 weeks): add bulkheads isolating B-bound traffic, priority-based queue admission, load shedding at the producer when 429 share exceeds a threshold, and capacity modeling that treats dependency quota — not worker count — as the throughput constraint. Re-run the 09:20-style scaling experiment in staging to confirm workers no longer scale into a hard ceiling. Validate all changes against E01-E10-style baseline metrics so regression is detectable.\\n\\n8. CONCLUSION\\n\\nDependency B's rate limiting was the primary cause; retry amplification and latency feedback were amplifiers; worker scaling failed because the bottleneck was external and quota-bound, not local.
